channel.title: Integrations on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Integrations on Best of AI

item.title: Ambience Healthcare
item.description:
Ambience builds AI for the paperwork around medical care. With patient consent, its system captures the conversation between clinician and patient, then generates a structured note in the clinician’s preferred format. The clinician reviews and signs it, which cuts the time spent charting after hours.

Its distinct focus is coding and compliance. From the same conversation and the chart, the tool suggests diagnosis and procedure codes with supporting evidence, which can reduce missed codes and billing errors. Because of that, it targets health systems and large practices rather than single clinicians, and it works with different specialties.

item.title: Boomi
item.description:
Boomi was one of the first cloud integration platforms. Its visual builder lets teams connect applications and move data between them, with a large catalog of connectors, API management, data integration, and workflow automation in one platform. Companies use it to sync records between sales, finance, HR, and operations systems without extensive custom code.

The company has leaned into AI agents. Boomi lets teams build agents that use connected systems as tools, and offers an agent catalog and controls to track what agents are allowed to do, which matters as companies deploy many of them. Data management and master data tools help keep records consistent across systems.

item.title: Dropbox Sign
item.description:
Dropbox Sign lets people sign documents without printing them. You upload a file, mark where each signer needs to sign or fill in fields, and send it by email. Signers open it on any device, sign, and the finished copy is stored with an audit trail that shows who signed and when. Templates make repeat documents such as contracts and NDAs quick to send.

The product started as HelloSign and was acquired by Dropbox, which renamed it. It connects with Dropbox storage, Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft tools, and CRM systems, so documents can be sent from where they already live. A developer API lets software companies embed signing flows inside their own products, and Dropbox has added AI features in its wider document tools.

item.title: Kore.ai
item.description:
Kore.ai helps large organizations deploy virtual assistants. Companies design conversations and workflows in a low-code environment, connect them to back-end systems, and publish them on websites, mobile apps, messaging platforms, and voice lines. The assistants can answer questions and complete tasks such as resetting a password or checking a balance.

The platform has moved from rule-based dialogue to generative AI and agents. It supports large language models from several providers, retrieval over company content, and tools for building multi-agent systems, with governance features for testing and monitoring. Prebuilt solutions for banking, healthcare, retail, and HR speed up projects, and agent assist tools support human staff on live calls.

item.title: Meltano
item.description:
Meltano treats data integration like software development. A project defines extractors and loaders in a configuration file, and Meltano runs them to move data from sources into a warehouse. Because everything is code, pipelines live in Git, run in CI, and can be reviewed like other changes.

It builds on the Singer standard, which has hundreds of community connectors, and integrates with dbt for transformations and Airflow for orchestration. Teams can write custom connectors with a software development kit, which is handy for sources that commercial tools do not cover.

item.title: Qlik
item.description: Qlik is known for its associative engine, which treats all the data in an app as connected. When you click a value in a chart, everything else updates to show related data, and values that are unrelated are shown as excluded, which helps users discover connections they did not think to query. This differs from tools that require predefined queries and has been a selling point for business users exploring data.

item.title: Vidyard
item.description:
Vidyard is a video platform for business teams. Salespeople record quick webcam or screen videos for prospects, send them by email or link, and see who watched and for how long. Marketers host videos on their websites with branded players and gated forms.

AI features speed up production. Script suggestions help with what to say, avatars let a rep send a personalized video without recording each one, and transcripts, summaries, and chapters make longer videos easier to use. Integrations with Salesforce and HubSpot put engagement data in the CRM.

item.title: Careforce AI
item.description:
Careforce provides AI workers for healthcare administration. Agents place outbound calls and texts to patients, such as to schedule overdue screenings, confirm appointments, and collect information before a visit. They handle follow-up and rescheduling, which often falls through in busy offices.

The company says its agents support many languages and can work across scheduling systems and payer portals, which lets clinics reach patients who might otherwise be missed. Scripts are configurable for different campaigns, such as preventive care outreach and post-operative check-ins.

item.title: Veo 2
item.description:
Veo 2 generated short high-resolution clips from text or image prompts. It stood out for understanding cinematic language, such as lens choices and camera moves, and for physics that looked plausible, with fewer odd distortions.

It was offered through Google’s creative tools and API before being succeeded by Veo 3, which added native audio and further improvements. Many users moved to the newer model for quality and sound.

Check Google’s documentation for the currently supported models. Alternatives include Veo 3, Runway, Kling, Luma, and Pika. Veo 2 is of interest mainly to people comparing generations of video models.

item.title: AgentOps
item.description: AgentOps addresses a problem specific to AI agents: they make many decisions, call tools, and chain model requests, which makes failures hard to understand. By adding a few lines of code, developers record each agent session, and the platform shows a timeline of prompts, model responses, tool calls, and errors. A replay view lets you walk through exactly what the agent did, which helps find why it looped, hallucinated, or failed to finish.

item.title: ChurnZero
item.description:
ChurnZero is built for customer success teams at software-as-a-service companies. It pulls in product usage data, support tickets, and CRM information to give each account a health score, so a team can see which customers are thriving and which are at risk of leaving before a renewal conversation turns bad.

Automation handles routine outreach. Playbooks trigger tasks and emails when a customer hits a milestone or goes quiet, in-app messages guide users inside the product, and dashboards track renewals, adoption, and revenue. AI features summarize accounts, draft messages, and suggest next actions, and a customer-facing portal can share progress with clients.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: Eden AI
item.description:
Eden AI addresses the problem of integrating many AI vendors. Each provider has its own API, formats, and billing. Eden AI offers one API for tasks like text generation, translation, OCR, speech recognition, image analysis, and more, and routes the request to the provider a developer chooses.

That makes comparison simple: the same input can be sent to several providers to see which gives the best result for the price. Fallback options switch to another provider if one fails, and a single bill and dashboard track usage. Workflows allow chaining several AI steps.

item.title: Highspot
item.description:
Highspot helps sales organizations make sure reps find and use the right material. Marketing publishes decks, case studies, and playbooks in one library, reps search or get recommendations based on the deal stage and customer, and managers see which assets are used and which correlate with wins.

Training and coaching tools are part of the platform, including practice exercises, call reviews, and guided selling plays. AI features recommend content, summarize accounts, and generate tailored messages and presentations. Integrations with CRMs and communication tools bring this into reps’ daily workflow.

item.title: Kommunicate
item.description:
Kommunicate combines a chatbot builder with a shared inbox for agents. Businesses add a chat widget to their site or app, train a bot on help articles and FAQs, and let it answer routine questions, handing the conversation to a person when the bot cannot help or the customer asks.

The platform supports generative AI models and connects to knowledge bases, so answers draw on company content. Multi-channel support extends to messaging apps, and analytics show deflection rates and satisfaction. Integrations with CRMs and helpdesks keep data in sync.

item.title: Landbot
item.description:
Landbot lets non-developers design conversations visually. A user drags blocks onto a canvas to ask questions, branch based on answers, and connect to other tools, then publishes the flow on a website, a landing page, or WhatsApp. The conversational format often gets more responses than a plain form.

AI features add the ability to answer free-text questions from a knowledge base and to build flows from a description. Integrations send leads to CRMs and spreadsheets, and handoff routes complex chats to human agents. Templates cover lead generation, support, and onboarding.

item.title: Letta
item.description:
Letta grew out of the MemGPT research project, which proposed managing an agent’s memory like an operating system manages memory. In Letta, an agent has a core memory it always sees and external stores it can read and write, so it can keep information across conversations that far exceed a model’s context window.

Developers create agents through an API, define their tools and memory blocks, and let them run over long periods. This suits assistants that need to remember user preferences, companions, and agents that learn from experience. A hosted platform manages deployment, and tools let developers inspect and edit what an agent remembers.

item.title: Lindy
item.description:
Lindy lets people create agents without code. A user describes a task or chooses a template, connects apps like Gmail, Slack, and a CRM, and defines triggers and steps. The Lindy then runs on its own: sorting an inbox, drafting replies, booking meetings, or updating records.

Workflows can include several steps with conditions, and Lindies can hand tasks to each other or ask a human for approval. A phone agent product handles calls, and a large catalog of integrations connects to business tools.

item.title: MLflow
item.description:
MLflow began at Databricks as a way to bring order to machine learning work. Teams log parameters, metrics, code versions, and artifacts for each run, compare results in a web interface, and package models in a standard format that can be deployed in many environments. A model registry manages versions and stages.

The project has extended to generative AI. It supports tracing of LLM applications, evaluation tools, and prompt management, making it useful for teams building with language models as well as classic models. It works with most ML libraries and cloud platforms.

item.title: Navattic
item.description:
Navattic helps companies show software without a live demo. A marketer captures a product’s screens or pages, adds callouts and steps, and publishes a tour that visitors can click through. Gated or ungated, these demos let prospects see the product before talking to sales.

Analytics show who viewed a demo and how far they went, giving sales a signal about interest. Personalization lets teams tailor tours by account, and integrations send engagement data to CRMs and marketing tools. AI helps create and edit demos and write copy.

item.title: Phrasee
item.description:
Phrasee focuses on the words in marketing messages. A team sets up a brand voice, and the platform generates many variations of subject lines, push text, or ads, predicts which will perform best, and tests them against audiences. Results feed back to improve future suggestions.

The company has become part of Jacquard Group, which combines it with other brand messaging tools. Large retailers, financial institutions, and travel brands used it to squeeze more from large campaigns, where small improvements in open rate add up.

item.title: Rewatch
item.description:
Rewatch is built on the idea that useful knowledge is trapped in recordings no one rewatches. It captures meetings and async videos, transcribes them, and organizes them into channels and playlists, so employees can find the moment they need by searching words said.

Features include summaries, chapters, comments on moments in the video, and integrations with Zoom, Slack, and calendars. The goal is to let people catch up on meetings quickly and reduce the number of live sessions.

item.title: ScrapeGraph AI
item.description:
ScrapeGraph AI lets developers describe what they want from a page. A user supplies a URL and a prompt such as list every product name and price, and the library fetches the page, passes it to a language model, and returns structured data. It also builds graph pipelines for multi-page scraping.

The approach reduces the brittleness of selector-based scrapers, which break when layouts change. It supports local and cloud models, and a hosted API and no-code options exist.

item.title: Smartling
item.description:
Smartling connects content systems to translators. Websites, apps, and documents flow in through integrations, and Smartling applies translation memory and machine translation, then routes text to human linguists where quality matters most. Translations return to the source system.

Features include visual context for translators, glossaries, quality scoring, and AI that translates and edits at scale. The company has pushed AI-first workflows to reduce cost and time, and reports on translation quality and spend.

item.title: Transifex
item.description:
Transifex helps product teams translate content into many languages. Developers connect repositories such as GitHub and GitLab, or use a command-line tool, and new text is sent to Transifex for translation. Translators and reviewers work in an online editor with translation memory, glossaries, and context, and approved translations flow back to the codebase.

A distinctive piece is Transifex Native, which lets apps fetch translations through an SDK, so updating a translation doesn’t require a new release. AI and machine translation pre-translate content, and quality checks flag issues, while workflows route text through reviewers or professional translation vendors. Integrations cover design tools, content management systems, and help centers.

item.title: Amwell
item.description:
Amwell provides the technology behind a lot of virtual care. Hospitals and health systems use it to run telehealth programs for their own patients, health plans offer it as a benefit, and employers use it to give workers access to remote visits. Patients can see a clinician by video for urgent care, primary care, behavioral health, and specialty care, with scheduling, intake, and visit tools in one platform.

It also offers services around the visit. These include a hospital-grade platform for remote consultations within hospitals, digital programs for chronic conditions, and a network of clinicians for companies that don’t have their own. AI features help with intake, triage, and documentation, and the platform integrates with electronic health records. Its ability to be customized for each client is a selling point.

item.title: Applitools
item.description: Applitools solves a problem that ordinary automated tests miss: whether a page looks correct. A functional test can confirm a button exists while the layout is broken, overlapping, or off-screen. Applitools Eyes takes screenshots during tests and compares them to approved baselines using a visual AI that understands layout, text, and color the way a person would. That avoids the flood of false alarms from pixel-by-pixel comparison, where tiny rendering differences trip every check.

item.title: Arcadia
item.description:
Arcadia has two sides. For consumers, it helps people use renewable energy even if they cannot install solar panels. Customers subscribe to a share of a local community solar project and receive credits on their utility bill, or choose plans that match their usage with renewable generation. The platform tracks bills and savings in one account.

For businesses, Arcadia offers access to utility data. It connects to thousands of utilities to pull bill and usage information through APIs, which energy software companies, solar developers, and sustainability teams use to analyze consumption. This data layer is a major part of its business and helps other companies build energy products.

item.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud
item.description:
Autodesk Construction Cloud brings together the tools that general contractors, owners, and subcontractors use to run building projects. A shared data environment keeps drawings, models, and documents in one place with version control, so everyone works from the current set. Teams use it for design review, model coordination across disciplines, quantity takeoff, cost estimating, issue tracking, and quality and safety checks in the field.

Autodesk has been folding the product line into Forma, its industry cloud, and the construction products now carry the Forma name, such as Forma Build, Forma Data Management, Forma Takeoff, and Forma Estimate. They connect to Autodesk’s design tools like Revit, which keeps information flowing from the design model to the construction site. AI features help automate routine work and surface insights, for example by flagging risks, extracting information from documents, or speeding up takeoff.

item.title: Avalara
item.description: Avalara helps businesses get indirect taxes right. Sales tax rules vary by state, city, product type, and customer, and rates change often, which makes manual calculation risky. Avalara integrates with online stores, accounting software, and ERP systems to calculate the correct tax at checkout or invoicing based on the transaction’s location and product, then helps file returns and remit payments in many jurisdictions. It covers sales and use tax, VAT, and other transaction taxes around the world.

item.title: Character Creator
item.description: Character Creator lets artists build 3D characters without modeling every detail. You start with a base body, adjust shape sliders for face and body, and apply skin, hair, clothing, and accessories from a library. A rigged skeleton and facial controls come ready to animate, so a character can be used right away in games, films, and animations. Pipelines to Unreal Engine, Unity, Blender, Maya, and other tools make it practical in production.

item.title: Crowdin
item.description:
Crowdin helps teams make products available in many languages. Developers connect their repositories, such as GitHub or GitLab, and Crowdin picks up new source strings, makes them available to translators, and syncs completed translations back, so localization keeps pace with development. It works with files from mobile, web, and game projects, and with content from design tools like Figma and from help centers.

The translation environment supports several workflows. Professional translators, in-house reviewers, and community volunteers can work in an editor with context, screenshots, glossaries, and translation memory that reuses past translations for consistency. Machine translation and AI features pre-translate content and suggest improvements, and quality checks catch errors. Project managers track progress and can order work from translation vendors through the platform.

item.title: CVAT
item.description: CVAT was created at Intel and released as open source, and is now maintained by a company called CVAT.ai along with a community. It is a web-based tool for labeling data for computer vision: drawing bounding boxes, polygons, polylines, points, and masks, and tagging images or video frames with classes. It handles tasks such as object detection, segmentation, tracking across video, and classification, and exports to common formats such as COCO, YOLO, and Pascal VOC.

item.title: Drata
item.description:
Drata addresses the burden of proving security compliance. Companies selling to enterprises are often asked for a SOC 2 report or other certifications, and preparing for an audit traditionally takes months of gathering screenshots and documents. Drata connects to systems such as AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, Okta, and HR tools, automatically checks whether controls are in place, and collects evidence continuously, so the company remains audit-ready.

The platform covers more than evidence. It manages policies and employee training, tracks vendor risk, supports risk assessments, and offers a trust center that lets customers see a company’s security posture. Auditors can work directly in the platform. AI features help fill out security questionnaires, summarize risks, and map controls across multiple frameworks, saving time for small security teams.

item.title: Draw.io
item.description:
Draw.io is a free tool that handles a surprising range of diagrams. It offers shape libraries for flowcharts, UML, entity relationships, network and cloud architecture, floor plans, and more, with smart connectors and alignment guides that keep drawings tidy. Because there is no account requirement, you can open it, draw, and save without signing up. Many software teams use it for documentation diagrams.

A defining feature is where your files live. You can save diagrams to your device, to Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, GitHub, or GitLab, instead of a vendor’s server, which suits organizations with strict data rules. Diagrams export to PNG, SVG, PDF, and other formats, and can be embedded in Confluence, Jira, Notion, and other tools through plugins. You can also create diagrams from text by inserting Mermaid or PlantUML code.

item.title: Finch3D
item.description:
Finch3D addresses the early design stage, when architects test many layout ideas against requirements. You define a building footprint or site, along with rules such as unit mix, room sizes, and circulation, and Finch generates floor plan options that satisfy the constraints and optimizes them for factors like area efficiency. Architects can compare alternatives quickly instead of sketching each by hand.

The tool is built to fit architects’ workflows. It integrates with the design software they already use, including Revit, Rhino, and Grasshopper, so generated layouts can be refined and documented in familiar environments. It supports quick iterations when the brief changes, and provides metrics that help justify choices to clients, such as the number of units or usable area.

item.title: Geotab
item.description:
Geotab makes the small devices that plug into vehicles and report what they do. A device in the diagnostic port records location, speed, harsh braking, idling, engine fault codes, and more, and sends the data to the cloud, where fleet managers view it on maps and dashboards. Companies with delivery vans, service trucks, buses, and long-haul trucks use it to track vehicles, optimize routes, and reduce costs.

Analytics turn the data into insights. Driver scoring identifies risky behavior and supports coaching, maintenance alerts flag vehicles that need service based on engine data, and fuel and emissions reports support efficiency and electric vehicle planning. AI features include an assistant that answers questions about fleet data in natural language, and models that predict problems and rank safety risks. A marketplace of third-party apps extends the platform, and compliance tools support electronic logging rules.

item.title: Mabl
item.description: Mabl aims to make automated testing less fragile. Teams record or describe user flows, such as signing in or checking out, and the platform turns them into automated tests that run in the cloud across browsers and devices. A low-code approach means QA engineers and developers can create tests without writing everything in code, though scripting is available when needed. Tests run on a schedule or in CI/CD pipelines when code changes.

item.title: MindMeister
item.description:
MindMeister helps you think in branches. You start with a central topic and add connected ideas around it, using keyboard shortcuts to build a map quickly. Maps can be formatted with colors, icons, images, links, and notes, rearranged freely, and turned into outlines. People use it for brainstorming, studying, project planning, meeting notes, and mapping out content such as articles or courses.

Collaboration is a core strength. Several people can edit a map at once, with comments and voting to gather input, and maps can be shared by link. A presentation mode turns a map into slides, and tasks can be assigned on map nodes and synced with the project tools in the same suite. Integrations connect with Google Workspace, Microsoft Teams, and other apps, and exports include PDF, image, and Word formats. AI features suggest ideas and generate map structures from a topic.

item.title: MonkeyLearn
item.description:
MonkeyLearn let people analyze text without machine learning expertise. Teams could connect support tickets, survey responses, reviews, and social posts, pick a ready-made model for sentiment or topics, or train a custom classifier by tagging examples. Results appeared in dashboards and could be sent to spreadsheets, helpdesks, and BI tools, which made it popular with customer experience, product, and marketing teams.

Its approach was to make natural language processing approachable. A visual interface handled model creation and testing, and the API let developers add analysis to their own apps. Typical uses included tagging support requests by issue, tracking sentiment in reviews, and pulling themes from open-ended survey answers.

item.title: Readwise
item.description:
Readwise addresses a common frustration: highlighting passages and never seeing them again. It imports highlights from Kindle, Apple Books, Instapaper, Pocket-style services, podcasts, and PDFs into one library, and sends a daily review of a few of them by email or in the app, using spaced repetition so important ideas return at intervals.

The service integrates with the note-taking ecosystem, exporting highlights to Notion, Obsidian, Roam, Logseq, and others, so notes stay linked to sources. Search lets you find a highlight across everything you have read, and a mobile and browser extension make capture easy. Readwise also makes Reader, a read-it-later app, and AI features can summarize and let you chat with your highlights.

item.title: Spacemaker AI
item.description:
Spacemaker was a Norwegian startup that applied AI to the first phase of building design. Given a site and a set of goals, it generates many layouts for buildings, then analyzes each for sunlight, daylight, wind comfort, noise, views, and the amount of floor area it provides. Designers can compare options and adjust parameters, rather than testing a few ideas by hand.

Autodesk acquired the company and integrated its technology into Autodesk Forma, a cloud platform for early design. Forma combines site context, environmental analysis, and design tools, and connects to Revit and other Autodesk products so early decisions can be carried into detailed design. The platform serves architects, developers, and city planners evaluating projects.

item.title: Stripe
item.description: Stripe began as a way for developers to accept card payments with a few lines of code and has become the payment layer for much of the internet. Businesses use it to take cards and local payment methods online and in person, bill customers on subscription plans, send invoices, and pay out sellers on marketplaces. Its documentation and libraries are widely admired, which is why startups tend to adopt it first. It operates in many countries and currencies.

item.title: TaxJar
item.description:
TaxJar tackles the complexity of U.S. sales tax for online businesses. Rules differ by state, county, and city, and a seller can owe tax in many places once they pass certain thresholds. TaxJar connects to selling channels such as Shopify, Amazon, WooCommerce, and BigCommerce, pulls in sales data, calculates the tax owed, and shows where the business has obligations. Reports summarize what is due in each jurisdiction.

The service can also file and remit returns in many states for an additional fee, which saves sellers from dealing with each state’s portal. An API provides tax calculations at checkout for platforms and developers. It was acquired by Stripe, which has been building its own tax product, Stripe Tax, and TaxJar continues to operate and support filing, while its role is evolving alongside Stripe’s tools.

item.title: Testim
item.description:
Testim addresses one of the biggest pain points in test automation: tests that break whenever the interface changes. Instead of relying on a single brittle identifier for each element, it uses machine learning to learn multiple attributes of each element, so the test can still find a button after a developer renames or moves it. This self-healing behavior reduces the time engineers spend fixing tests.

Tests can be recorded by clicking through an app, then edited visually or with code for custom logic. The platform runs tests in the cloud across browsers and integrates with CI/CD tools, issue trackers, and test management systems, so test results fit into existing workflows. Features such as grouping and reusable steps help teams scale suites, and AI assists with test creation and failure analysis.

item.title: Ada
item.description: Ada helps companies handle customer support questions without adding staff. Its AI agent answers inquiries on websites, in apps, and over messaging channels by drawing on a company’s knowledge base and systems, and it can take actions such as checking an order, changing an address, or processing a return by connecting to back-end tools. When a request is too complex or sensitive, it hands the conversation to a human agent with context.

item.title: AI For Developer
item.description:
AI For Developer is a niche directory focused on the developer audience. Instead of listing every AI product, it gathers tools that matter to people who write software: coding assistants, AI-powered editors, model APIs, testing and documentation tools, and infrastructure for building AI features. Listings give a short description, links, and categories, which makes it easy to browse by use case.

Directories like this serve as a starting point for discovery. They help developers learn what exists, compare similar tools, and keep up with the rapid pace of new launches. A curated approach aims to reduce the noise of general AI directories that include thousands of products across every field, by focusing on relevance to engineering.

item.title: Airbyte
item.description: Airbyte solves the data movement problem. Data teams use it to pull information from applications, databases, and APIs, such as Salesforce, Postgres, Stripe, and Google Ads, and load it into destinations such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks, on a schedule. Hundreds of pre-built connectors cover common sources, and a low-code builder, with AI assistance, lets teams create connectors for others. Because it is open source, the connector catalog grows with community contributions.

item.title: Amazon CodeWhisperer
item.description:
CodeWhisperer was Amazon’s first coding assistant, a counterpart to GitHub Copilot that suggested lines and whole functions as you typed in editors such as VS Code and the JetBrains IDEs. It was trained with a special focus on AWS APIs, so it was particularly good at code that called S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other AWS services. It also supported many popular programming languages.

Two features set it apart from early rivals. A reference tracker flagged suggestions that resembled open-source code and showed the license, and a security scan checked your code for vulnerabilities such as exposed credentials and injection flaws. An individual tier was free, and a professional tier added admin controls and higher limits.

item.title: Avoma
item.description: Avoma joins sales, customer success, and recruiting meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then records and transcribes them and produces notes organized by meeting type. Instead of a generic summary, it uses templates suited to the call, such as a discovery call or a customer check-in, and pulls out action items, objections, and next steps. Notes and key fields can be pushed into CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot, which saves reps from doing data entry after every call.

item.title: Botkeeper
item.description:
Botkeeper offered accounting firms a way to scale bookkeeping with automation. Its software connected to clients’ accounting systems, categorized transactions with machine learning, reconciled accounts, and prepared financial statements, with human reviewers checking the work. The aim was to let firms serve more clients with the same staff and to reduce routine data entry.

The company raised substantial funding, but it shut down after losing a large share of its revenue when major customers were acquired and changed their arrangements. It then sold its Infinite AI platform to Xendoo, a bookkeeping firm, which said it would keep the platform active and supported as its own division. The long-term roadmap is less clear, and customers had to decide whether to move.

item.title: Charisma.ai
item.description:
Charisma.ai helps creators combine writing with generative AI. Instead of leaving a character entirely to a language model, creators design a story with scenes, goals, and character personalities, and the platform lets characters respond flexibly to what players say while steering the conversation along the intended narrative. This approach aims to keep stories coherent and on message, which is a common problem with free-form AI dialogue.

Tools include a visual story editor, character memory and emotion systems, voice and animation integration, and SDKs for Unity, Unreal, and web apps. The platform has been used for games, interactive entertainment, branded experiences, and training simulations where conversation practice is valuable. Writers can control tone and limits while still giving players freedom.

item.title: Climate FieldView
item.description:
Climate FieldView helps farmers use their data. With a device plugged into farm equipment, FieldView Drive collects information about planting, applications, and harvest, and the data syncs to the cloud, where farmers view maps of their fields, compare hybrids and practices, and analyze yield. Satellite imagery tracks crop health during the season, and weather data and field notes add context.

Advanced features support planning. Variable-rate prescriptions tell equipment to apply seed and fertilizer at different rates across a field based on zones, which can improve efficiency, and scripts or models estimate the profitability of decisions. Integrations with equipment and other agriculture software reduce manual data transfers. Machine learning supports yield predictions and recommendations.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit acts as a first reviewer. When a developer opens a pull request, it reads the diff along with surrounding code, writes a summary of the change, and leaves comments on potential bugs, missing tests, security concerns, and style. Developers can reply to its comments and ask it to explain or fix things, so the review becomes a conversation.

Configuration lets teams set rules and instructions in plain language so the review follows their standards. It learns from feedback, and can run linters and security scanners as part of the review. IDE and command line versions bring review earlier, before a pull request is opened.

item.title: CodeRabbit
item.description:
CodeRabbit gives every pull request a quick first review. When a developer opens a pull request, it summarizes the change, walks through the files, and leaves comments on potential bugs, security problems, performance concerns, and deviations from team conventions. It can also suggest fixes that developers apply with a click and answer questions in the comments, acting like a tireless reviewer available at any hour.

It improves with use. CodeRabbit learns from how reviewers respond to its suggestions and from guidelines the team defines, so comments become more relevant over time. It runs linters and security scanners as part of its review, can use context from the wider codebase, and has an IDE and command-line version for reviewing before code is pushed. It integrates with issue trackers to check that changes match requirements.

item.title: Composio
item.description:
Composio is an integration layer for AI agents. Agents need to take actions in other software, which means handling authentication and API details for each service. Composio supplies a catalog of connectors that handle sign-in flows and expose actions in a form models can call, so a developer can give an agent access to many apps with a few lines of code.

It works with agent frameworks and model providers, supports the Model Context Protocol, and manages user authorization so that agents act on behalf of each end user. Tools for monitoring let developers see what actions agents took, and permissions limit what an agent can do.

item.title: Copyleaks
item.description:
Copyleaks checks text for originality. It compares documents against web pages, publications, and its own databases to find copied passages, and it also estimates whether text was written by an AI model. Schools, publishers, and businesses use it to check student work, submissions, and content.

It supports many languages and file types, and integrates with learning management systems so teachers can scan assignments in their usual workflow. Reports show matched sources and highlight text flagged as likely AI-written. Additional tools cover code plagiarism and a writing assistant.

item.title: Expensify
item.description:
Expensify is known for making expense reports less painful. Employees photograph receipts or forward them by email, SmartScan extracts the merchant, date, and amount, and the app builds a report for submission. Managers approve in the app, and approved expenses sync to accounting software.

Other features cover company spending. The Expensify Card gives employees corporate cards with real-time receipts matching, policies flag out-of-bounds expenses automatically, and mileage tracking and per diems handle travel. AI helps categorize spending and spot policy issues.

item.title: Fireflies.ai
item.description: Fireflies sends a bot into your meetings, usually named Fred, that records the call and creates a transcript with speaker labels. After the meeting, it produces a summary with action items and key topics, and posts them where your team works. Every meeting becomes searchable text, so you can find what a customer said last month or when a decision was made. It supports dozens of languages and works with the main video call platforms and uploaded recordings.

item.title: Flowise
item.description:
Flowise lets people assemble AI applications visually. In its canvas, you connect nodes representing models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools into a flow, test it in a chat window, and expose it through an API or an embedded widget. It started as a visual layer over LangChain and LlamaIndex and has grown to include agent flows with branching, loops, and human approval steps.

Typical uses include chatbots that answer from company documents, customer support assistants, and agents that call APIs and tools. It supports many model providers, including local models through Ollama, and many vector databases, which gives teams a choice about where data and compute live. Because it is open source, it can be self-hosted, and the project has a strong community and many templates.

item.title: Make
item.description: Make, formerly called Integromat, lets you automate work between apps by drawing it. You place modules on a canvas for each app, such as Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, or a CRM, and connect them with lines that show how data flows. You can add routers that split the flow into branches, filters that decide which items continue, iterators that handle lists, and functions that change data on the way. This visual layout makes complicated logic easier to follow than a long linear list of steps.

item.title: MeetGeek
item.description:
MeetGeek joins your calendar’s online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript and summary after each one. The summary lists decisions, action items, and key points, and highlights flag important moments. Notes are sent automatically to attendees or to tools like Slack, Notion, HubSpot, and Google Docs, which cuts down on manual write-ups.

Beyond a single meeting, it organizes knowledge across your calls. Hubs group meetings by team or topic, and you can search past conversations or ask questions about them. Meeting templates tailor summaries for sales calls, interviews, or team check-ins, and analytics show participation and talk time. Teams can get insights into patterns across customer calls.

item.title: n8n
item.description: n8n lets you build automations by connecting nodes on a canvas, similar to Zapier or Make, but with more room for code. Each node is a step: a trigger like a webhook or schedule, an action in an app, or a block that transforms data with JavaScript or Python. Hundreds of integrations are included, and a generic HTTP node covers the rest. Workflows can branch, loop, and call other workflows, so it handles anything from simple notifications to elaborate data pipelines.

item.title: Netlify
item.description:
Netlify popularized the idea of pushing code to Git and having a site build and deploy automatically. Developers connect a repository, and Netlify builds on each change, gives every pull request a preview URL, and serves the site from a global network. Serverless functions and edge functions add dynamic behavior without servers.

The platform has added AI features. Agent Runners let AI agents such as Claude and Codex make changes to a site and open pull requests, and an AI-oriented gateway and tooling help developers use models inside their projects. Forms, identity, and storage services handle common needs.

item.title: Notta
item.description: Notta turns speech into text for people who sit through many conversations. You can record in the mobile or web app, upload audio and video files, or let its assistant join Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams calls. The transcript appears in the app with speaker labels and timestamps, and you can search it, edit it, and share it. It supports a large number of languages, which suits international teams, journalists, and researchers.

item.title: Noty.ai
item.description:
Noty.ai is a lightweight tool for people who want meeting notes without much setup. It records and transcribes online meetings, then creates a summary that highlights the main discussion points, decisions, and tasks. The goal is to let participants focus on the conversation instead of typing, and to give everyone a shared record afterward.

Its integrations make the notes easy to reuse. Summaries can be pushed to Notion and other workspace tools, and the transcript is searchable, so you can find what was said about a topic in a past meeting. A browser extension handles recording in Google Meet and Zoom, and a free plan lets individuals try the product.

item.title: Nuance DAX
item.description: DAX, short for Dragon Ambient eXperience, was developed by Nuance and later acquired by Microsoft. With patient consent, the system captures the conversation between clinician and patient, uses speech recognition and AI to turn it into a structured medical note in the format the clinician needs, and sends it to the electronic health record for review and signature. The goal is to cut the hours doctors spend on documentation and let them focus on patients.

item.title: Open WebUI
item.description:
Open WebUI gives people a familiar chat interface for models they control. You run it on your own server or computer, connect it to local models through Ollama or to any OpenAI-compatible API, and get a polished web app with conversation history, model switching, prompt libraries, and voice input. It started as a front end for Ollama and has become a full platform.

Features target teams and power users. Retrieval-augmented generation lets users upload documents and chat with them, web search can add current information, and tools and functions extend what models can do. Administrators can manage multiple users, roles, and permissions, which suits organizations that want an internal AI assistant without sending data to a third party. It supports plugins and pipelines for custom behavior.

item.title: Palantir Gotham
item.description:
Gotham helps organizations that work with sensitive and scattered data make decisions. It pulls information from many systems, such as databases, reports, sensor feeds, and documents, into a unified model of people, places, events, and relationships, called an ontology. Analysts can search, visualize connections, map activity, and collaborate on investigations, and operational users can plan and track missions.

The platform is used in defense, intelligence, and public safety. Capabilities include link analysis, geospatial views, timelines, and tools for managing access to classified or restricted data, and it can run in secure and air-gapped environments. Palantir’s Artificial Intelligence Platform adds large language models that work with the same data under access controls, allowing users to ask questions and automate analysis.

item.title: Phrase
item.description:
Phrase helps companies translate software and content into many languages. Developers connect repositories and design tools, and new text is sent to translators or machine translation, then returned to the product when approved. Translation memory reuses earlier work and glossaries keep terminology consistent.

The platform brings together several products that grew from a merger: a translation management system, a string management tool for software teams, and a computer-assisted translation editor. AI translation engines and quality estimation reduce the amount of human review needed for lower-risk content.

item.title: Plaid
item.description: Plaid connects apps to bank accounts. When you link an account in a budgeting app, investment platform, or payments service, Plaid’s interface asks you to sign in to your bank, and the app then receives only the data you permit. Developers use Plaid’s APIs to verify account ownership, check balances, read transaction history, confirm identity, assess income and assets for lending, and initiate transfers, without building separate integrations with thousands of banks.

item.title: Qodo AI
item.description:
Qodo started as CodiumAI with a focus on tests, and has expanded to quality across the development process. In the IDE, it analyzes a function, understands its behavior, and generates unit tests that cover normal cases, edge cases, and failure modes, which helps developers raise coverage without writing everything by hand. It also offers chat and code suggestions that take the project context into account.

The review side is a major part. Qodo Merge, built on an open-source tool called PR-Agent, comments on pull requests with summaries, potential bugs, security issues, and suggested fixes, and can learn a team’s standards so reviews reflect internal rules. Multi-agent review systems and a context engine aim to understand large codebases, which matters for enterprise teams with many repositories. Integrations cover GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and major IDEs.

item.title: Scholarcy
item.description:
Scholarcy tries to make reading faster. You give it an article or upload a PDF, and it breaks the document into a summary card with key points, the main findings, study design, limitations, and important terms. It extracts figures, tables, and references, and links the references so you can follow them. The format helps readers decide whether a paper is worth a full read.

A browser extension summarizes papers on publisher websites, and a library stores summaries with notes and tags. Export options send content to reference managers and note apps, and a feature can generate flashcards for study. Students and researchers use it to process large reading lists, create literature review notes, and check key details quickly.

item.title: Shopify
item.description: Shopify lets someone start an online store without building the software behind it. You choose a theme, add products, set up payments and shipping, and the platform handles hosting, the checkout, and tax and currency settings. The same system also covers in-person sales through point-of-sale hardware, so a shop can manage online and physical inventory together. Everything from a one-person side business to large brands runs on it, and Shop Pay, its accelerated checkout, is used well beyond Shopify’s own stores.

item.title: Siri
item.description: Siri is the assistant that comes with every Apple device. You say “Hey Siri” or hold a button, then ask it to send a message, set a timer, call someone, play music, adjust a setting, or control HomeKit devices. It works across Apple’s hardware, so the same assistant is on your wrist, in your car through CarPlay, and on a smart speaker. Its biggest advantage is how deeply it ties into the system, since it can act on messages, calendars, reminders, and photos without extra setup.

item.title: SmolAgents
item.description: SmolAgents is designed to be easy to read and use. The core logic fits in a small amount of code, and building an agent takes a few lines: you pick a model, give it tools, and run a task. Its signature idea is the code agent, where the model writes its actions as Python code instead of structured tool calls. This lets it combine steps, use loops and variables, and handle multi-step problems efficiently, and the approach often needs fewer steps than traditional methods.

item.title: Sourcegraph Cody
item.description: Cody grew out of Sourcegraph’s code search, which indexes entire repositories and lets developers find and understand code across many projects. That context was its main advantage: instead of guessing from the open file, Cody could draw on the broader codebase to answer questions, write code that matched existing patterns, and explain how parts of a system fit together. It worked in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and the web, with chat, autocomplete, and commands to edit and test code.

item.title: Supabase AI
item.description:
Supabase provides what an application needs behind the scenes. It gives developers a hosted Postgres database with auto-generated APIs, user authentication, file storage, real-time updates, and serverless edge functions, all manageable from a web dashboard. It’s often described as an open-source alternative to Firebase, with the advantage of using standard SQL and a portable database.

For AI, Supabase supports the pgvector extension, which stores embeddings in Postgres and enables similarity search, so developers can build semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation without a separate vector database. Edge functions can call language models, and an AI assistant in the dashboard helps write SQL and design schemas. It has become a popular backend for AI app builders such as Lovable and Bolt.

item.title: Supermaven
item.description: Supermaven was a coding assistant that focused on one thing: fast, accurate autocomplete. Its main claim was an unusually large context window, which let it consider much more of your project than most completion tools when suggesting the next lines. Developers liked how quickly suggestions appeared, and extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and Neovim made it easy to try. A free tier and a low-priced paid plan helped it spread.

item.title: Tabnine
item.description:
Tabnine was one of the earliest AI code completion tools, and it built its identity on privacy and control. It works inside VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and other editors, suggesting lines and functions, answering questions in chat, writing tests and documentation, and explaining code. A distinguishing choice was letting companies run it in their own environment, including fully disconnected networks, and keeping code out of any third party’s training.

Its enterprise pitch centers on context. Tabnine can learn from a company’s repositories, style guides, and standards so suggestions match internal conventions, and administrators can choose which models are used, including options hosted in-house. It offers attribution and provenance controls for companies worried about generated code resembling open-source projects with restrictive licenses. Agents extend it to larger tasks such as code review and test generation.

item.title: Todoist
item.description: Todoist is a clean, fast task manager. You add tasks by typing in plain language, like “send report every Friday at 3pm,” and it turns that into a recurring due date. Tasks can be organized into projects and sections, given priorities and labels, and viewed as a list, board, or calendar. Filters let you build views such as everything due today across all projects. It syncs across phones, computers, browsers, and email clients.

item.title: Unbounce AI
item.description:
Unbounce helps marketers create landing pages that convert. A drag-and-drop builder and templates make it possible to publish pages without developers, with popups and sticky bars to capture leads on websites. Marketers connect pages to ad campaigns and test variants to find what performs best.

AI is a core part. Smart Copy generates headlines and body text from a brief, and Smart Traffic uses machine learning to send each visitor to the variant they are most likely to convert on, based on their attributes, which can improve results faster than a standard A/B test. Newer tools analyze pages and suggest improvements, and AI builder features create a page from a prompt.

item.title: Vapi
item.description:
Vapi handles the hard parts of voice agents. Developers define an assistant with a prompt and tools, connect a phone number, and Vapi orchestrates speech-to-text, the language model, and text-to-speech, with handling for interruptions and turn-taking. Bring-your-own provider choices allow swapping components.

Use cases include customer support lines, appointment scheduling, outbound calls, and voice assistants in apps. The platform includes testing, analytics, and call transfer features.

Vapi is billed by minutes plus provider costs. Voice calls are regulated, and callers should know they are speaking with an AI. Alternatives include Retell AI, Bland AI, Synthflow, Twilio ConversationRelay, and LiveKit. Vapi suits developers building voice agents.

item.title: Vertex AI
item.description: Vertex AI is where Google Cloud customers build with AI. At its center is Model Garden, a catalog that includes Google’s Gemini, Imagen, and Veo models, open models like Llama and Gemma, and models from partners such as Anthropic. You can call a model through an API, test it in a studio, and then deploy it with Google Cloud’s security, networking, and compliance controls. Data stays under the customer’s governance, which matters for regulated industries.

item.title: W&B Weave
item.description:
Weave addresses a common problem with LLM apps: it is hard to know what they are doing. Adding a few lines of code logs each call with its inputs, outputs, latency, cost, and the surrounding function calls, so a developer can inspect a failing response step by step instead of guessing. The traces cover nested calls, which matters for agents that chain several models and tools.

It also handles evaluation. Teams build datasets of test cases, define scorers (including LLM judges), and run experiments to compare prompts, models, and app versions before shipping. Results are tracked over time, which makes it easier to tell whether a change actually helped. Online evaluations can score live traffic and flag regressions in production.

item.title: Wolfram Alpha AI
item.description: Wolfram Alpha doesn’t search the web. It computes answers. Ask it to integrate a function, convert units, compare populations, or show the weather on a given date, and it uses curated data and algorithms, written in the Wolfram Language, to produce a result with steps, charts, and data. That makes it reliable for math, physics, chemistry, statistics, and factual queries with definite answers, which is where language models often make mistakes.

item.title: Zed AI
item.description:
Zed is built for speed. Its editor, written in Rust, starts quickly and stays responsive on large projects, and multiplayer editing lets several people work in the same file with voice and chat.

AI is built in rather than added by extension. Users chat with models in an assistant panel, ask for inline edits, and run an agent that edits code across files, with support for several providers and local models. Edit predictions suggest the next change as you type, and the Agent Client Protocol lets other agents run inside.

item.title: Aide
item.description: Aide was an AI-first code editor from the London startup CodeStory. It was a fork of VS Code, so it looked familiar and could use extensions, but it added a layer of AI that understood the project. You could chat about the codebase, ask for changes across several files, and get completions informed by wider context. It was released as open source under the AGPL license, and the project drew substantial interest from developers looking for an alternative to Cursor.

item.title: Beehiiv
item.description:
Beehiiv is built for people who run newsletters as a business. Writers compose and send posts, manage subscriber lists, and publish a website for the archive. Growth tools include referral programs, recommendations between newsletters, and landing pages, which help build an audience without outside ads.

Monetization is a central feature. Creators can sell paid subscriptions, run ads through the Beehiiv ad network, add sponsors, and offer digital products. Analytics show opens, clicks, and which posts convert readers. An AI assistant helps with drafts, subject lines, and ideas, and automation handles welcome sequences.

item.title: Botpress
item.description: Botpress started as an open-source tool for building chatbots with visual flows, and it grew into a platform around large language models. Developers and technical teams build agents that talk with customers on websites and messaging channels, connect to knowledge bases, and call APIs to do things like check an order or update an account. A visual builder and code options sit side by side, so non-engineers can adjust conversations while developers handle integrations.

item.title: ClearML
item.description:
ClearML helps machine learning teams keep their work organized and reproducible. Adding a couple of lines of code to a training script logs parameters, metrics, code versions, and outputs to a central server, so experiments can be compared and repeated. This replaces scattered notebooks and manual notes.

The suite goes beyond tracking. It includes dataset versioning, a task queue that sends jobs to available machines, pipelines that chain steps together, and model serving. For companies with expensive GPUs, resource scheduling shares hardware across teams. ClearML also supports orchestration for large language model workflows.

item.title: Comet ML
item.description:
Comet helps machine learning teams track and compare their work. A few lines of code log metrics, parameters, code, and datasets from training runs to a dashboard, where experiments can be compared and reproduced. A model registry stores approved versions and their lineage.

Production monitoring watches deployed models for drift and performance changes. For generative AI, Comet created Opik, an open-source tool for tracing and evaluating language model applications, which brings it into the same space as other LLM observability products.

item.title: Copysmith
item.description:
Copysmith targets online retailers that need lots of product copy. A merchant can generate descriptions for many products from a spreadsheet or catalog, create ad headlines and text, and draft emails and social posts. Bulk generation saves time when a store has hundreds of items.

Integrations connect it to Shopify and Google Ads, so content can flow into the tools where it is used. Team features allow collaboration and approval, and brand settings keep tone consistent. Some tools support SEO optimization by suggesting keywords.

item.title: Factory AI
item.description:
Factory sells AI agents for engineering teams. Droids take tasks from tickets or chat, explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and open pull requests for review. Specialized droids handle different jobs, such as code review, incident response, or migrations.

The product works through a command line tool, IDE integrations, and a web interface, and connects to GitHub, Jira, Slack, and other tools so agents fit into existing workflows. Enterprise features address security, permissions, and model choice, with support for several model providers.

item.title: LanceDB
item.description:
LanceDB is a database for AI data. It stores vectors alongside the original data, such as text, images, and video references, and supports similarity search, filtering, and full-text search. Because it is embedded, it runs inside an application with no server, similar to how SQLite works for relational data.

The Lance format makes it efficient for large datasets: it keeps data on disk, supports versioning, and allows fast random access, so it can handle collections that do not fit in memory. A cloud and enterprise offering adds scalability and managed service. It is used for retrieval in AI applications and for managing training data.

item.title: Mastra
item.description:
Mastra targets JavaScript and TypeScript developers who build AI features. It provides building blocks: agents that call tools, workflows with steps and branching, retrieval over documents, memory, evaluations, and observability. Developers can run it locally with a playground to test and debug.

Its design fits the web stack, with deployment options for serverless platforms and integration with frameworks like Next.js. It works with models from many providers through a common interface and supports the Model Context Protocol. A hosted platform offers deployment and monitoring.

item.title: Nabla
item.description:
Nabla works as a scribe in the exam room. During a visit, with consent, it captures the conversation and creates a structured note in the clinician’s preferred format, which they review and copy into the health record. It also drafts letters and patient instructions from the same encounter.

The company began in France and has expanded to the United States and elsewhere, with support for multiple languages and specialties. It emphasizes privacy, including not retaining audio after processing, and integrates with electronic health record systems.

item.title: Paragraph AI
item.description:
Paragraph AI brings AI writing to the smartphone. A user types a few words or dictates an idea, and the app produces a full email, message, or post, which can be adjusted for tone, length, or formality. Rewrite and proofreading tools tidy existing text.

The appeal is convenience for writing on the go, when opening a full desktop assistant is awkward. Typical uses include replying to emails, drafting social captions, and polishing short messages.

item.title: Refact.ai
item.description:
Refact.ai gives developers an assistant they can control. It offers autocomplete, chat that understands the codebase, and an agent that can carry out tasks like fixing bugs, running tests, and refactoring. It plugs into popular editors.

Privacy is a key benefit: companies can run it on their own servers with open models so code never leaves their environment, or use cloud models. Fine-tuning on a codebase is available in some setups.

item.title: Voiceflow
item.description:
Voiceflow lets teams design conversational agents together. On a visual canvas, designers and developers map out how an agent should respond, add steps that call language models, search knowledge bases, run logic, and connect to APIs and tools. Non-engineers can shape conversations while developers handle integrations, which makes it practical for cross-functional teams in customer support, sales, and operations.

The platform handles the whole lifecycle. You can add a knowledge base of company content so the agent answers from it, test the agent in a built-in environment, and deploy it to a website, messaging channels, phone lines, or via API. Analytics and transcripts show how conversations go, and versioning and collaboration features support teamwork. Voiceflow works with a choice of language models.

item.title: Weaviate
item.description:
Weaviate stores objects and their vector embeddings together. Applications query by meaning, filter by metadata, and combine vector similarity with keyword search. It can create embeddings itself through integrated modules or accept vectors from outside.

Generative search lets a query retrieve relevant objects and pass them to a language model in one step, which suits retrieval-augmented generation. Multi-tenancy, replication, and compression support production use at scale. Weaviate can be self-hosted or used as a managed cloud service.

item.title: Wordware
item.description:
Wordware treats prompts as code. Users write workflows in an editor that feels like a document, mixing instructions in plain language with structure for loops, branches, and tool calls. The aim is to let people who understand a problem, not only engineers, build AI apps.

Workflows can be published as apps or APIs, and the platform supports several model providers and integrations. Teams use it for research agents, content workflows, and internal tools.

item.title: ZenML
item.description:
ZenML helps teams move ML work from notebooks to production. Developers write pipelines as Python functions, and ZenML runs them on a chosen orchestrator, such as Kubeflow, Airflow, or a cloud service, tracking artifacts and metadata along the way.

A stack concept separates pipeline code from infrastructure, so the same pipeline can run locally during development and in the cloud in production. The framework has extended to support LLM workflows and agents.

item.title: Adobe Express
item.description:
Adobe Express is Adobe’s answer to Canva: a simple editor where you start from a template, change the text and images, and export. It covers social media posts, banners, flyers, simple videos, and quick edits to PDFs. It runs in the browser and on phones, and it needs no design background. Brand kits, shared templates, and a content scheduler help small teams keep their posts consistent.

The AI tools come from Adobe’s Firefly models. You can generate images from a text prompt, extend or fill parts of a photo, apply text effects from a description, remove backgrounds, and resize a design for several platforms in one step. Because it shares libraries with Creative Cloud, assets from Photoshop or Illustrator can be used directly in Express projects, and designers can hand off a template that colleagues then adjust.

item.title: Bing Image Creator
item.description: Bing Image Creator made AI image generation easy to try. You type a description, and it returns several images within a few seconds, with no installation and no cost beyond a Microsoft account. Its popularity came from being free and being available inside Bing and Edge, long before many alternatives had a free tier. Microsoft has since renamed the tool Image Creator from Designer and tied it into Copilot and the Designer app.

item.title: BlogSEO
item.description:
BlogSEO aims to automate the path from keyword to published post. A user enters a topic or website, the tool finds relevant keywords, creates an outline based on what ranks, and drafts an article. Some workflows can schedule and publish posts directly to a content management system.

For small businesses without a writer, that can mean a steady flow of blog content. The risk is that generic, unedited AI articles rarely rank well and can weaken a site’s credibility. Search engines favor original, helpful pages, so the strongest use is to draft quickly and then add real expertise, examples, and fact-checking.

item.title: JetBrains AI Assistant
item.description: JetBrains AI Assistant works inside the IDEs that many professional developers already use. In IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, and the rest of the family, it provides inline completion, a chat panel that understands the project, and actions to explain code, generate tests, write commit messages, and suggest fixes for errors. Because it is built into the IDE, it can use the IDE’s deep knowledge of code structure, such as types, references, and run configurations.

item.title: Litmaps
item.description: Litmaps helps researchers see a field instead of reading a list. You start with one or more papers you know, and the tool plots them on a map where one axis shows publication date and the other shows how much a paper is cited. Lines between the nodes show citation links. From the seeds, it suggests related papers that cite or are cited by your set, so you can quickly find missing foundational works and recent developments.

item.title: Logseq
item.description: Logseq is built on the idea that notes should be a network of connected blocks. You write in an outliner where each bullet is a block, link to other pages with double brackets, and see backlinks that show everywhere an idea is referenced. Daily journals are the default entry point, so you capture thoughts as they come and organize them through links instead of folders. A graph view shows how pages relate.

item.title: Luminar Neo
item.description: Luminar Neo is built for photographers who want strong results without a lot of manual work. Instead of slider-heavy workflows, it offers AI tools that do the hard parts in a click. Sky AI replaces or enhances skies, Relight AI changes the lighting in a scene using depth information, Portrait Bokeh AI creates background blur, and tools for skin, face, and body adjustments handle portraits. Generative tools can erase objects and expand the canvas.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot
item.description: Microsoft uses the Copilot name for a family of assistants rather than one product. The consumer Copilot app and website work like other AI chatbots: you can ask questions, generate text and images, talk by voice, and have it look at your screen or camera for help with what you are doing. It is built into Windows and the Edge browser, where it can summarize pages, compare information across open tabs, and help with tasks as you browse.

item.title: Pipedream
item.description: Pipedream sits between no-code automation and writing everything yourself. You build workflows from triggers, such as a webhook or a new row in a sheet, and steps that either call a prebuilt action for an app or run your own code, with access to npm and PyPI packages. That mix lets developers move faster than in tools like Zapier while still handling logic that needs real programming, and it suits integrations and internal automations.

item.title: Reflect
item.description:
Reflect aims to be a quick place to capture thoughts and connect them. You write notes, link them to each other with simple syntax, and see backlinks that show where an idea is referenced. Daily notes serve as an inbox, a calendar view ties notes to meetings, and a graph helps visualize connections. The app is built for speed and a clean interface, with sync across devices.

The AI assistant works on your notes. It can summarize a page, rewrite text, brainstorm, and answer questions based on the content you have saved, and voice transcription turns spoken notes into text. Reflect also emphasizes privacy: notes are end-to-end encrypted, which limits what the company can see. Browser extensions and integrations let you save web content and connect with services like Kindle highlights and Readwise.

item.title: Robin AI
item.description:
Robin AI developed tools for lawyers who spend their days reading contracts. Its platform used language models trained on legal text to review agreements, flag risks, suggest edits to bring them in line with a company’s playbook, and answer questions about clauses. It worked in Microsoft Word and was used by in-house legal teams and law firms for routine commercial agreements such as NDAs, supplier contracts, and sales terms.

The company also combined software with a managed legal services offering, in which lawyers reviewed work and handled volume for clients. That mix aimed to deliver quick, reliable turnaround, with AI doing the first pass and humans checking. It gained attention for fast growth and for partnerships and funding in the legal AI boom.

item.title: Slack AI
item.description:
Slack AI addresses the problem of catching up. When you return from time off or join a busy channel, it can summarize what happened, list decisions, and highlight what needs your attention. Thread summaries cut long discussions into a few lines, and daily recaps cover channels you choose, so you can stay informed without reading every message.

AI search turns Slack into a place to ask questions. Instead of hunting for keywords, you can ask something like what the timeline is for a project, and receive an answer drawn from messages, files, and connected apps, with links to the sources. Slackbot is being reshaped as an assistant that can help draft messages, find information, and take actions, and Salesforce’s Agentforce agents can work in Slack. Huddle notes summarize audio calls.
